courses.subject: Hydrology
courses.lead: How water moves over and under the land — from a raindrop to a river. We follow the order of a first hydrology course.
outline: Time of concentration and the rational method

notes.title: The hydrologic cycle
notes.tldr: Water is never used up. The same water keeps moving between the ocean, the air, the land surface and the ground, lifted by the sun's energy and pulled back down by gravity.

figure.caption: The hydrologic cycle. Orange arrows are water going up as vapour, teal arrows are liquid water moving down and sideways.

blocks.p: The sun evaporates water from the ocean and from the land. Wind carries the vapour, it cools and condenses into clouds, and it falls again as **precipitation** (rain or snow).

On land, a falling drop has several possible paths. Some is caught on leaves and evaporates again (**interception**). Some soaks into the soil (**infiltration**). What the soil cannot take in flows over the surface to a stream (**surface runoff**). Water in the soil is either taken up by roots and returned to the air through leaves (**transpiration**), or it moves further down to the groundwater (**percolation**). Groundwater moves slowly and seeps into rivers, which is why a river keeps flowing long after the rain has stopped (**baseflow**). Rivers carry the water back to the ocean, and the loop closes.

Hydrology is bookkeeping with two kinds of numbers. A **store** is how much water is in one place (a volume, or a depth in mm). A **flux** is how fast water moves from one store to another (a volume per time, or mm per day). Mixing the two up is the most common beginner's mistake.

The stores are very unequal. About 97% of the Earth's water is salt water in the oceans, and only about 2.5% is fresh. Of that fresh water, roughly 69% is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers and about 30% is groundwater. Rivers and lakes, the water we actually see and use, hold well under 1% of the fresh water.
How long does a water molecule stay in a store on average? Divide the size of the store by the flux through it.

where: volume of water in the store
flux through the store (volume per time)

blocks.p: Small stores with a large flux turn over fast (the atmosphere: days). Large stores with a small flux turn over slowly (deep groundwater: hundreds to thousands of years; the ocean: about 3,000 years). This is why polluted groundwater takes so long to recover, and why rainfall can change within hours.

Korea receives about 1,300 mm of precipitation in an average year, roughly 1.6 times the average over the world's land. But more than half of it falls between June and September, and the rivers are short and steep, so the water arrives all at once and leaves quickly. Floods in summer and shortages in spring are two sides of the same cycle.

example.q: The atmosphere holds about 12,900 km³ of water at any moment. Global precipitation is about 577,000 km³ per year. How long does water stay in the air on average?
example.a: About 8 days. All the water in the air is replaced roughly 45 times a year.

mistakes: **Thinking of one big loop.** The cycle is many loops of different sizes. About 90% of the water that evaporates from the ocean falls straight back onto the ocean.
**Picturing groundwater as an underground river or lake.** It is water filling the small pores of soil and rock, and it usually moves metres per day or less.
**Confusing a store with a flux.** 'A lot of water' in a lake (a store) says nothing about how much flows through it (a flux).
notes.ours: Floods and droughts are the two extremes of this cycle: too much water arriving too fast, or too little for too long. Our work on hydrologic modelling, climate extremes, AI-based forecasting and satellite observation is all about measuring and predicting the fluxes drawn in this figure.

check.q: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water?
check.a: In ice sheets and glaciers (about 69%), then in groundwater (about 30%). Rivers and lakes together hold far less than 1%.

check.q: It has not rained for three weeks, but the river still flows. Where does the water come from?
check.a: From groundwater seeping into the channel (baseflow). Groundwater is a large, slow store that keeps releasing water between storms.

notes.title: The watershed
notes.tldr: A watershed is all the land that drains to one point on a river. It is the unit in which hydrologists count water.

figure.caption: A watershed seen from above. Rain falling inside the dashed divide ends up at the outlet; rain falling outside flows to a neighbouring river.

blocks.p: Pick any point on a river and call it the **outlet**. Now ask: if it rains, from which land will the water flow downhill to this point? That land is the **watershed** of the outlet (also called a catchment or drainage basin).
Its edge is the **drainage divide**, which follows the ridges. A drop falling just inside the divide goes to our outlet; a drop falling just outside goes to the neighbour.

A watershed is defined by its outlet. Move the outlet downstream and the watershed grows, so watersheds are nested: the watershed of a small tributary (a **sub-basin**) sits inside the watershed of the main river.

On a contour map, start at the outlet and walk uphill, always crossing the contour lines at right angles, until you reach a ridge. Follow the ridges around and come back down to the outlet on the other side.
Today a computer does this from a digital elevation model (DEM): for every grid cell it finds the steepest downhill neighbour, then collects all the cells whose water eventually reaches the outlet.
Besides the area $A$, two simple numbers say a lot about how a watershed responds to rain.

where: drainage density (km of stream per km²)
length of the basin along the main stream

ul: **Area** sets the volume: the same storm on twice the area gives twice the water.
**Drainage density** sets the speed: with many streams, water has a short way to go over the slow hillslope before it reaches a fast channel.

**Shape** sets the timing: in a round basin, water from all parts arrives at the outlet at about the same time and makes a high, sharp peak. In a long, narrow basin the arrivals are spread out and the peak is lower.
**Slope** also matters: steep basins respond faster.

blocks.p: Water in Korea is managed by river basin, not by city or province: the Han, Nakdong, Geum, Yeongsan and Seomjin rivers. Our campus in Daejeon lies in the Geum River basin; rain falling here drains through Gapcheon stream into the Geum.

example.q: A watershed has an area of 120 km². The streams on the map add up to 180 km, and the basin is 20 km long along the main stream. Find the drainage density and the form factor.
steps: For comparison, a circular basin has $R_f = \pi/4 \approx 0.79$.
example.a: Drainage density is 1.5 km/km² and the form factor is 0.30, so this basin is clearly elongated. We expect a longer, flatter flood wave than from a round basin of the same area.

mistakes: **Using an administrative boundary.** Water does not follow city limits. A water balance only works inside a real drainage divide.
**Forgetting the outlet.** 'The watershed of the Geum River' has no fixed area until you say where on the river you stand.
**The word itself.** In American English a watershed is the area; in British English it is the dividing line. In Korean, 유역 is the area and 분수계 is the line.
**Assuming groundwater follows the surface divide.** Usually it roughly does, but in some geology (limestone, for example) groundwater crosses under the ridge.
notes.ours: Every flood forecast or drought analysis begins by choosing a watershed. Rainfall from gauges, radar or satellites is averaged over it, a hydrologic model turns that rainfall into flow at its outlet, and the prediction is checked against the gauge at that outlet.

check.q: You move the outlet downstream, past the point where a tributary joins. What happens to the watershed?
check.a: It grows: it now also includes the whole watershed of that tributary.

check.q: Two basins have the same area and receive the same storm. One is round, the other long and narrow. Which has the higher peak flow?
check.a: The round one. Water from all parts of it reaches the outlet at about the same time, so the flows add up into a sharp peak.

notes.title: The water balance
notes.tldr: What comes in, minus what goes out, equals the change in what is stored. It is conservation of mass applied to a watershed, and it is the most used equation in hydrology.

figure.caption: A watershed as a container. Precipitation is the input; evapotranspiration and streamflow are the outputs; the difference changes the storage.

blocks.p: Draw a boundary (a watershed) and choose a period (a storm, a month, a year). Water cannot appear or disappear, so whatever entered and did not leave must still be inside.

where: change in storage (soil water, groundwater, snow, lakes and reservoirs)

blocks.p: If the watershed also exchanges water in other ways, such as groundwater crossing the divide, water pumped in or out, or a transfer from another basin, those terms are added in the same way.
Rain is measured as a depth (mm) and streamflow as a volume per time (m³/s). To compare them, turn everything into a **depth over the watershed area** for the chosen period:
A handy fact: 1 mm of water over 1 km² is 1,000 m³.

Over many years, storage goes up and down but does not keep growing, so $\Delta S \approx 0$ and the balance becomes $P = Q + ET$. This gives the standard way to estimate the evapotranspiration of a whole basin, which nobody can measure directly: $ET = P - Q$.

Over a single storm or month, storage is the main character. After a dry spell the first rain mostly refills the soil and little reaches the river. The same rain on soil that is already wet becomes a flood. A drought is a long period in which storage keeps falling.
The share of precipitation that leaves as streamflow, $Q/P$, is called the **runoff ratio**.

example.q: A 250 km² watershed receives 1,300 mm of precipitation in a year. The mean flow at its outlet is 4.5 m³/s. Estimate the annual evapotranspiration and the runoff ratio, assuming the storage is the same at the start and end of the year.
example.a: About 730 mm of evapotranspiration and a runoff ratio of 0.44: a little under half of the precipitation becomes streamflow.

mistakes: **Mixing units.** Subtracting m³/s from mm is the classic error. Convert every term to mm over the watershed first.
**Setting ΔS = 0 for a short period.** It is a fair assumption over many years, a poor one for a single month, and wrong for a single storm.
**Forgetting people.** Dams, pumping, irrigation and transfers between basins are real terms in many balances.
**Trusting the balance more than the data.** Every term carries a measurement error, and all of those errors end up in whichever term you solve for.
notes.ours: A hydrologic model is a water balance repeated at every time step, with rules for how water moves between the stores. When we assess a drought or forecast a flood, we are tracking this balance, with rainfall from gauges, radar and satellites as the input.

check.q: A storm drops 50 mm on a 10 km² watershed. What volume of water is that?
A basin has P = 1,200 mm and Q = 500 mm in an average year. Estimate ET.
check.a: ET = P − Q = 700 mm, taking the long-term storage change as zero.

notes.title: Measuring precipitation
notes.tldr: A rain gauge measures rain directly but only at one point. Radar and satellites see rain everywhere but only indirectly. Good rainfall data combine them.

figure.caption: Three ways to observe the same storm. The gauge catches the water itself; radar and satellites measure a signal and convert it to a rain rate.

blocks.p: Rainfall is reported as a **depth**: how deep the water would stand on a flat surface if none ran off or soaked in (mm). Depth per time is the **intensity** (mm/h). Precipitation is the input to every hydrologic calculation, so an error here passes through to everything that follows.

A gauge is a funnel of known opening that collects rain. The common automatic type is the **tipping-bucket gauge**: a small bucket tips over each time it fills with a fixed amount (0.1 to 0.5 mm), and the times of the tips give the intensity.

A gauge is the most direct measurement we have, but it has two limits. First, it catches a little too little: wind carries drops past the opening (a few percent for rain, far more for snow), and a tipping bucket loses some water in very heavy rain. Second, and more important, it is a point. Rain varies a great deal over a few kilometres, especially in summer thunderstorms, and a gauge cannot see what falls between gauges.
A radar sends out microwave pulses and listens for the echo from raindrops. The strength of the echo is the **reflectivity** $Z$. It is turned into a rain rate $R$ with an empirical relation:

where: reflectivity (mm⁶/m³), usually given in dBZ = 10 log₁₀ Z
constants; the classic Marshall–Palmer values are a = 200, b = 1.6

blocks.p: Radar gives a map of rain about every kilometre and every few minutes, out to 100–250 km. But it is indirect: $a$ and $b$ depend on the sizes of the drops, which change from storm to storm; mountains block the beam; and far from the radar the beam is high above the ground, so it sees rain that may change before it lands.

Satellites estimate rain from the radiation they receive: infrared sensors see how cold (how high) the cloud tops are, microwave sensors respond to the drops and ice inside the cloud, and a few satellites carry a radar. Merged products such as GPM IMERG give rain every 30 minutes on a grid of about 10 km for nearly the whole globe, including oceans and regions with no gauges. The price is a larger error at the scale of a small watershed.

No single source is enough. In practice, gauges are trusted for the amount, radar and satellites for the pattern in space, and the two are merged: the remote-sensing field is corrected so that it agrees with the gauges where gauges exist.

example.q: A radar measures 40 dBZ over your watershed. Using the Marshall–Palmer relation, what rain rate is that? What about 50 dBZ?
example.a: About 12 mm/h at 40 dBZ and about 49 mm/h at 50 dBZ. Every extra 10 dBZ multiplies the rain rate by about 4, so a small error in reflectivity becomes a large error in rainfall.

mistakes: **Treating one gauge as the rainfall of an area.** A gauge opening about 20 cm across samples 0.03 m². With one gauge per 100 km², we measure roughly three ten-billionths of the area.
**Saying that radar measures rain.** It measures echo strength some height above the ground. The rain rate is an estimate built on assumptions.
**Expecting a radar pixel and a gauge to agree exactly.** One is an average over about 1 km² in the air, the other a point on the ground. Some disagreement is real, not an error.
**Confusing depth with intensity.** 30 mm in ten minutes and 30 mm in a day are very different events.
notes.ours: Rainfall is the first input of our flood and drought studies, so its quality limits everything after it. We work with gauge, radar and satellite rainfall, study how to combine them, and look at how their errors carry through hydrologic models and AI forecasts. Unusual sensors such as cameras and microphones are one more way to fill the gaps between gauges.

check.q: Why does a rain gauge usually read a little less than the true rainfall?
check.a: Mainly because wind deflects drops around the opening (much more so for snow). Wetting, evaporation and missed water during very heavy rain add smaller losses.

check.q: Two radar pixels show 30 dBZ and 40 dBZ. Roughly how do their rain rates compare?
check.a: The 40 dBZ pixel has about four times the rain rate (10 dBZ more multiplies R by 10^(1/1.6) ≈ 4.2 with Marshall–Palmer).

notes.title: Areal average rainfall
notes.tldr: A water balance needs one rainfall depth for the whole watershed. We get it from point gauges by giving each gauge a weight equal to the share of the watershed it represents.

figure.caption: Thiessen polygons for four gauges. Gauge D stands outside the watershed but is still the nearest gauge for the eastern corner, so it gets a small weight.

blocks.p: Gauges give rainfall at points, but the water balance asks how much fell on the whole watershed. The answer is a weighted average of the gauges. The methods differ only in how they choose the weights.

where: part of the watershed area assigned to gauge i
weight of gauge i (the weights add up to 1)

ul: **Arithmetic mean.** Add the gauges and divide by their number: every gauge gets the same weight. It is fine when the land is flat and the gauges are evenly spread, and poor otherwise.

**Thiessen polygons.** Every place in the watershed is assigned to its nearest gauge. Draw lines joining neighbouring gauges, then the perpendicular bisectors of those lines; the bisectors form a polygon around each gauge. The weight of a gauge is its polygon area inside the watershed divided by the watershed area. The weights depend only on where the gauges are, so they are computed once and reused for every storm.

**Isohyetal method.** Draw contour lines of equal rainfall (isohyets), and weight the average rainfall between two neighbouring isohyets by the area between them. It can follow real patterns, such as more rain on the mountains, but the map must be redrawn for every storm and depends on who draws it.

blocks.p: Modern practice does the same thing on a grid: rainfall is interpolated to every cell (by inverse-distance weighting or kriging) and the cells inside the watershed are averaged. With radar or satellite rainfall the grid already exists, and the areal average is simply the mean of the cells inside the divide.

example.q: A 200 km² watershed has the four gauges shown in the figure. Their Thiessen polygons cover 72, 66, 45 and 17 km², and a storm gives 42, 60, 75 and 30 mm. Find the areal average rainfall by the Thiessen method and by the arithmetic mean.
example.a: 54.3 mm by Thiessen and 51.8 mm by the arithmetic mean. The arithmetic mean is lower because it gives the dry outside gauge D a quarter of the weight, although D represents under a tenth of the area. The difference of 2.6 mm is about 520,000 m³ of water on this watershed.

mistakes: **Using the arithmetic mean with clustered gauges.** Gauges are usually where people live, in the valleys. In mountain basins a plain average then underestimates the rain.
**Ignoring gauges outside the watershed.** As the figure shows, an outside gauge can be the nearest one for part of the basin.
**Keeping the old weights when a gauge is missing.** If one gauge fails during a storm, the polygons of its neighbours change and the weights must be recomputed.
**Reading an areal average as a point value.** Averaging smooths the peaks: the basin-average intensity is lower than the highest intensity at any single gauge, and more so for large basins.
notes.ours: The same weighted average sits behind every basin rainfall series we use, whether it comes from a handful of gauges or from thousands of radar and satellite cells. Comparing these areal estimates with each other is one of the first checks we make before a rainfall product goes into a hydrologic model.

check.q: Can a gauge that stands outside the watershed have a Thiessen weight?
check.a: Yes. If some part of the watershed is closer to that gauge than to any other, that part belongs to its polygon.

check.q: Two gauges have Thiessen weights of 0.7 and 0.3 and record 20 mm and 50 mm. What is the areal average?

notes.title: Rainfall intensity, duration and frequency
notes.tldr: A storm is described by three numbers at once: how hard it rains, for how long, and how rarely such a storm happens. The IDF curve ties the three together, and it is where every design storm comes from.

figure.caption: Intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) curves for one site. Each curve is one return period. The marked point is the storm used in the worked example.

blocks.p: "It rained 60 mm" does not say much. 60 mm in one hour floods a city; 60 mm in a day is an ordinary wet day. So rainfall always needs a **duration**, and depth divided by duration is the average **intensity** (mm/h).

Two regular patterns show up in every rainfall record. For a longer duration, the average intensity is lower, because the heaviest burst never lasts long. And the rarer the storm, the higher the intensity. A plot of intensity against duration, with one curve for each level of rarity, is the **intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) curve**.

Two simple plots come first. A **hyetograph** is a bar chart of rainfall in each time step. A **mass curve** is the running total since the storm began; its slope at any moment is the intensity. To get the worst 60 minutes of a storm, slide a 60-minute window along the record and keep the largest total.
Rarity is expressed as a **return period** $T$: the average time between years in which a value is reached or exceeded. It is just another way to write a probability.

where: probability that the value is equalled or exceeded in any one year

blocks.p: A 100-year rainfall has a 1% chance of being exceeded in each year. It does not arrive every 100 years on schedule. Unit 15 shows how these values are estimated from the record.
For calculations the curve is fitted with a simple formula. A common one is the Talbot type:

where: constants for one site and one return period

blocks.p: Korean textbooks list several such forms: the Talbot type above, the Sherman type $I = c/t^{\,n}$ and the Japanese type $I = d/(\sqrt{t} + e)$. The rainfall depth for a given duration and return period is called the **probable rainfall** (확률강우량). In Korea these values are published for stations across the country and are the starting point of every flood design.

example.q: At one site the 10-year rainfall follows $I = 5{,}400 / (t + 30)$, with $I$ in mm/h and $t$ in minutes. Find the intensity and the depth for storms lasting 10, 60 and 120 minutes.
example.a: 135, 60 and 36 mm/h, or 22.5, 60 and 72 mm. As the storm gets longer the intensity falls but the total depth still grows. Which duration matters depends on the watershed: a small, fast basin reacts to the short, intense burst, a large one to the long storm (Unit 13).

mistakes: **Reading the return period as a schedule.** Two 100-year storms can fall in two years running. The return period is an average over a very long time.
**Stretching a short intensity.** 135 mm/h for 10 minutes does not mean 135 mm in an hour. Each duration has its own intensity.
**Using a point value for a large area.** IDF curves come from single gauges. The average over a watershed is lower, so the point rainfall is multiplied by an areal reduction factor (면적우량환산계수).
**Assuming the climate stands still.** The curves are fitted to past records. If heavy rain is becoming more frequent, yesterday's 100-year storm is no longer today's.
notes.ours: Design rainfall is where climate and engineering meet. A large part of our work on climate extremes asks how these curves are shifting, and how to estimate them when the record is short or changing, using long gauge records together with radar, satellite and climate-model rainfall.

check.q: What is the chance that a 50-year rainfall is exceeded in any one year?
check.a: p = 1/T = 1/50 = 0.02, or 2% in every year.

check.q: With I = 5,400 / (t + 30), what are the intensity and the depth of a 30-minute storm?
check.a: I = 5,400 / 60 = 90 mm/h, so the depth is 90 × 30/60 = 45 mm.

notes.title: Evapotranspiration
notes.tldr: Evapotranspiration is the water that goes back to the air, from open water, wet soil and the leaves of plants. It takes close to half of the rain, and it is the term of the water balance we can measure least directly.

figure.caption: Where the water leaves the land. Orange arrows are vapour; all of them need energy from the sun and air that can carry the vapour away.

blocks.p: **Evaporation** turns liquid water into vapour at a surface: a lake, wet soil, or rain caught on leaves. **Transpiration** is water that roots take from the soil and that leaves through small openings in the leaves. In the field we cannot separate the two, so we measure and model their sum, **evapotranspiration (ET)**.

ul: **Energy.** Turning water into vapour takes a great deal of heat, about 2.45 MJ for every kilogram. Almost all of it comes from the sun, so ET is high in summer and around midday.

**Dry, moving air.** Evaporation stops when the air above the surface is full of vapour. Dry air and wind keep carrying the vapour away. The measure of dryness is the gap between the vapour the air could hold and the vapour it holds now (the vapour pressure deficit).
**Available water.** A lake can always supply water. Soil cannot: when it dries, plants close their leaf openings and ET falls, however sunny the day.

blocks.p: **Potential evapotranspiration** is what would go up if water were never short; it depends only on the weather. **Actual evapotranspiration** is what really goes up, and it is equal to or less than the potential. In a wet month the two are close. In a drought the potential is high while the actual is low, and that gap is a useful sign of water stress.

ul: **Evaporation pan.** A shallow open pan of water (the standard Class A pan is about 1.2 m across); the daily drop in water level is read. A small pan heats up more than a lake, so it evaporates more, and the reading is multiplied by a **pan coefficient** of about 0.7.
**Water balance.** For a basin over many years, $ET = P - Q$ (Unit 3). For a block of soil with plants set on a balance (a lysimeter), the same idea works day by day.
**Energy balance.** The energy used for evaporation cannot exceed what the surface receives.

**Combination equations.** The Penman equation, and its successor the Penman–Monteith equation, combine the energy supply with the drying power of the air. They need only standard weather data: radiation, temperature, humidity and wind.

blocks.p: The pan gives the evaporation of a lake:
And the energy supply sets an upper limit:

where: net radiation received by the surface (energy per area per time)

blocks.p: 1 mm of evaporation over 1 m² is 1 kg of water, so it uses 2.45 MJ.

example.q: (a) A reservoir has a water surface of 3 km². A pan beside it loses 160 mm in July. Estimate the evaporation from the reservoir. (b) On a clear summer day the net radiation averages 150 W/m². What is the most that could evaporate?
steps: (b) Energy in one day: $150 \text{ W/m}^2 \times 86{,}400 \text{ s} = 12.96$ MJ/m².
example.a: (a) About 112 mm, or 336,000 m³ in one month. (b) At most about 5.3 mm/day. Real values are a little lower, because part of the energy heats the air and the ground instead.

mistakes: **Taking the pan reading as the lake evaporation.** The pan is small, shallow and warm. Without the coefficient the estimate is about 40% too high.
**Confusing potential with actual.** Formulas driven by weather give the potential value. On dry soil the actual value can be far lower.
**Treating ET as a small loss.** In Korea something like 40 to 55% of the annual precipitation returns to the air, and in a dry year the share is larger still.
**Expecting a direct measurement.** There is no gauge for the ET of a watershed. Every number is an estimate from a balance or a model, with an error to match.
notes.ours: Because ET cannot be gauged over an area, it is one of the things we estimate from satellites and models. It also decides how fast soil dries between storms, which is why it sits inside every hydrologic model we run and behind our drought analyses.

check.q: A pan loses 6 mm in a day. Roughly how much evaporates from the nearby lake?
check.a: About 0.7 × 6 = 4.2 mm.

check.q: The potential ET is 5 mm/day but the soil is very dry. Is the actual ET higher or lower than 5 mm/day?
check.a: Lower. Actual ET cannot exceed the potential, and when water is short the plants cut their water use.

notes.title: Infiltration
notes.tldr: Infiltration is rain soaking into the soil through the ground surface. It decides how rain is split: what soaks in feeds soil and groundwater, and what cannot soak in runs off and makes the flood.

figure.caption: Infiltration capacity during a steady, heavy rain. The capacity falls as the soil wets up; the rain above the curve has nowhere to go but over the surface.

blocks.p: Soil is full of small pores. Water enters them at the surface, pulled by gravity and by the suction of dry soil. The fastest rate at which a soil can take in water is its **infiltration capacity** $f$ (mm/h).

The actual rate depends on the rain as well. If the rain is lighter than the capacity, all of it soaks in. If it is heavier, the soil takes in water at its capacity and the rest collects on the surface and runs off.

Dry soil drinks fast: the pores are empty and the suction is strong. As the upper soil fills, the suction fades, and the capacity falls towards a steady value set by how easily water moves through the wet soil. Horton described this with an exponential curve:

where: initial capacity, at the start of the rain
final capacity, reached after a long rain

blocks.p: The area under this curve is the **cumulative infiltration**, the total depth that has entered the soil:

ul: **Soil texture.** Sand has large pores and a final capacity of tens of mm/h; clay may take only about 1 mm/h.
**Wetness before the storm.** The same soil takes in far less on the second day of rain than on the first.
**Land cover.** Forest soil is loose and protected by litter. Bare soil is sealed by the impact of raindrops. Pavement and roofs take in nothing.
**Compaction and frost.** Machinery, footpaths and frozen ground all close the pores.

blocks.p: In the field the capacity is measured with an infiltrometer: a ring pressed into the soil and kept filled with water, while the rate of supply is recorded. Besides Horton's curve, the Philip and Green–Ampt equations are widely used; they are derived from the physics of flow in soil.

example.q: A soil has $f_0 = 60$ mm/h, $f_c = 10$ mm/h and $k = 2$ per hour. It rains steadily at 60 mm/h for one hour. Find the capacity after one hour, the depth that infiltrates and the depth that runs off.
steps: The rain is at least as heavy as the capacity for the whole hour, so the soil takes in water at its capacity throughout.
example.a: The capacity drops from 60 to 16.8 mm/h within the hour. Of the 60 mm of rain, 31.6 mm soaks in and 28.4 mm runs off. Had the soil been wet at the start, with a capacity near 10 mm/h all along, about 50 mm would have run off.

mistakes: **Confusing capacity with rate.** Capacity is the most the soil can take. The actual rate is the smaller of the capacity and the rainfall intensity.

**Using Horton's curve in light rain.** The curve assumes water is always waiting at the surface. If the rain is lighter than the capacity, the soil wets more slowly and the capacity falls more slowly than the curve says.
**Treating infiltration as a constant.** The same field gives very different runoff on dry and on wet soil.
**Mixing up infiltration and percolation.** Infiltration is entry through the surface. Percolation is the movement further down, towards the groundwater.
notes.ours: The wetness of the soil before a storm is one of the largest sources of error in flood forecasting. Our hydrologic models track it between storms, satellites observe it from space, and it is one of the main reasons the same rainfall can give very different floods.

check.q: It rains at 5 mm/h on a soil whose capacity is 20 mm/h. How fast does water infiltrate, and is there surface runoff?
check.a: At 5 mm/h: all the rain soaks in, because the rain is lighter than the capacity. There is no surface runoff.

check.q: Why does the same 50 mm storm cause a larger flood in the middle of the rainy season than after a dry month?
check.a: The soil is already wet, so its infiltration capacity is close to the low final value. Less rain soaks in and more runs off.

notes.title: Effective rainfall
notes.tldr: Only part of a storm becomes a flood. Effective rainfall is that part: total rainfall minus the losses. Getting it right matters more than almost any later step of a flood calculation.

figure.caption: Two common ways to find the effective rainfall. Left: the Φ-index removes a constant loss rate from each hour. Right: the curve number method gives the runoff depth from the total storm rainfall.

blocks.p: When it rains, some water is caught on leaves, some fills small hollows in the ground, and much of it infiltrates. Together these are the **losses**. What is left reaches the stream quickly and is called the **effective rainfall** (also excess rainfall).
The key fact is a volume balance: the depth of effective rainfall, spread over the watershed, equals the volume of **direct runoff** in the flood hydrograph (Unit 11).

If the streamflow was measured, we know the depth of direct runoff. The Φ-index is the constant loss rate that makes the rainfall above it add up to that depth. It is found by trial: guess Φ, sum the rainfall above it, and adjust.

where: rainfall intensity in each time step (mm/h); only the steps with i larger than Φ are summed

blocks.p: In the figure the hourly rain is 10, 30, 20 and 5 mm and the measured direct runoff is 26 mm. With Φ = 12 mm/h the rain above the line is 18 + 8 = 26 mm, so Φ = 12 mm/h. Hours with less rain than Φ give no runoff at all.

For a watershed with no flow record, the most widely used tool is the curve number method of the US Soil Conservation Service (SCS, now NRCS). The whole watershed is summed up in one number, the **curve number** CN, between 0 and 100.

where: direct runoff, equal to the effective rainfall (mm)
potential maximum retention of the watershed (mm)
initial loss: rain that falls before any runoff begins

blocks.p: The retention $S$ follows from the curve number:
If $P$ is smaller than $0.2\,S$ there is no runoff. CN is read from tables, and it depends on three things:

ul: **Soil.** Four hydrologic soil groups, from A (sand, low runoff) to D (clay, high runoff).
**Land use and cover.** Forest and pasture have low values; paved city surfaces are close to 100.
**Wetness before the storm.** The antecedent moisture condition: AMC-I for dry, AMC-II for average and AMC-III for wet soil.

example.q: A storm drops 120 mm on a watershed. Find the effective rainfall when the watershed is mostly farmland and forest (CN = 75), and again after it has been built over (CN = 90).
example.a: 56.6 mm before and 91.7 mm after: the same storm gives about 60% more runoff from the built-up watershed. This is the main reason floods grow when a basin is urbanised.

mistakes: **Putting total rainfall into the unit hydrograph.** The unit hydrograph (Unit 12) works on effective rainfall only.
**Subtracting Φ from every hour.** In hours with less rain than Φ, the loss is the whole rain of that hour, not Φ. The effective rainfall cannot be negative.
**Reading CN as a measured property.** It is an empirical index. A change of a few points changes the runoff a great deal, so the choice has to be argued, not just looked up.
**Forgetting the wetness before the storm.** The same land has a higher CN after a week of rain.
notes.ours: Curve numbers come from soil and land-cover maps, and those maps now come largely from satellites. In our modelling work this step, deciding how much of the rain becomes runoff, is also where data-driven methods are often compared with the classical rules.

check.q: Hourly rainfall is 10, 30, 20 and 5 mm and the Φ-index is 12 mm/h. What is the effective rainfall in each hour?
check.a: 0, 18, 8 and 0 mm, which is 26 mm in total. The first and last hours are below Φ and give nothing.

check.q: A watershed has CN = 75. Does a 15 mm storm produce direct runoff?
check.a: No. The initial loss is 0.2 S = 16.9 mm, which is more than the 15 mm of rain.

notes.title: Measuring streamflow
notes.tldr: We cannot measure the flow of a river all the time. We record the water level all the time, measure the flow now and then, and link the two with a rating curve.

figure.caption: Left: one discharge measurement by the velocity–area method, with the numbers of the worked example. Right: many such measurements make a rating curve, which turns a water level into a discharge.

blocks.p: **Discharge** $Q$ is the volume of water passing a cross-section per second (m³/s). It is the product of the flow area and the mean velocity. Measuring it takes people, instruments and time, so it is done only occasionally. The **stage** $h$, the height of the water surface above a fixed mark, is easy to record every few minutes. Streamflow data are therefore built in three steps.

ul: **Record the stage continuously**, with a staff gauge read by eye, a float, a pressure sensor or a radar looking down from a bridge.
**Measure the discharge from time to time**, at low, medium and high water.
**Fit a rating curve** through the pairs of stage and discharge, and use it to turn the whole stage record into a discharge record.

blocks.p: In the **velocity–area method** the cross-section is cut into vertical strips. In each strip we measure the width $w$, the depth $d$ and the mean velocity $v$, and add up the flows of the strips.

Velocity changes with depth: it is slow near the bed and fastest just below the surface. A current meter therefore samples fixed points. In shallow water one reading at 0.6 of the depth below the surface is taken as the mean. In deeper water the mean of the readings at 0.2 and 0.8 of the depth is used.

Other methods follow the same logic. An acoustic Doppler profiler (ADCP) on a small boat measures velocities over the whole section in a few minutes. In floods, when nobody can enter the river, the surface velocity is taken from floats, a hand-held radar or video from the bank, and reduced by a factor of about 0.85 to get the mean.

where: stage at which the flow is zero

blocks.p: The curve is only as good as the measurements behind it, and they are scarce exactly where they matter most. Large floods are rare and dangerous to measure, so the top of the curve is usually an extrapolation. The curve also changes when the channel does: a flood can scour or fill the bed, and weeds grow in summer. It has to be checked every year.

example.q: A stream 6 m wide is divided into three strips of 2 m. The depths at the three verticals are 0.5, 1.2 and 0.8 m. The current meter gives 0.30 m/s at 0.6 of the depth in the first vertical, 0.70 and 0.50 m/s at 0.2 and 0.8 of the depth in the second, and 0.40 m/s at 0.6 of the depth in the third. Find the discharge.
steps: Mean velocity in the second vertical: $(0.70 + 0.50)/2 = 0.60$ m/s.
example.a: About 2.4 m³/s. The middle strip carries 60% of the flow, which is why real measurements use 20 or more verticals, placed closer together where the water is deep and fast.

mistakes: **Thinking the flow itself is recorded.** Almost every discharge value in a database was computed from a stage through a rating curve.
**Trusting flood peaks too much.** They come from the extrapolated part of the curve. An error of 20% or more in a flood peak is common.
**Using an old rating curve.** After a large flood the bed has moved, and the same stage no longer means the same discharge.
**Using the surface velocity as the mean.** The surface is the fastest part of the flow.
notes.ours: Observed discharge is what every model and every AI forecast is trained on and judged against, so its uncertainty sets the limit of what we can claim. Part of our work is finding better ways to observe rivers when gauging is difficult, from satellites and with cameras on the bank during floods.

check.q: A rating curve is Q = 20 (h − 0.5)², with Q in m³/s and h in m. What is the discharge at a stage of 1.5 m, and at 2.5 m?
check.a: At 1.5 m: 20 × 1.0² = 20 m³/s. At 2.5 m: 20 × 2.0² = 80 m³/s. One more metre of water gives four times the flow.

check.q: A vertical is 2.0 m deep. At which depths below the surface is the velocity measured with the two-point method?
check.a: At 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 m and 0.8 × 2.0 = 1.6 m. The mean of the two readings is used.

notes.title: The hydrograph
notes.tldr: A hydrograph is the flow of a river plotted against time. Its shape is the watershed's answer to a storm, and reading it is the first skill of flood hydrology.

figure.caption: A flood hydrograph and its parts, with the numbers of the worked example. The bar at the top is the effective rainfall that caused it.

blocks.p: Stand at the outlet of a watershed during a storm and write down the flow every hour. The plot of those values is the **hydrograph**. It rises when the fast water arrives, reaches a peak, and falls back slowly as the watershed drains.

blocks.h: The parts of a flood hydrograph

ul: **Rising limb.** The flow climbs as water from more and more of the watershed reaches the outlet. Its steepness depends mostly on the storm.
**Peak.** The largest flow, the number that decides whether a levee holds.

**Recession (falling limb).** After the rain stops, the water stored on the slopes, in the channels and in the soil drains away. Its shape depends on the watershed, not on the storm, so it looks much the same after every flood.

blocks.p: Three times describe the shape. The **lag time** runs from the centre of the effective rainfall to the peak. The **time to peak** runs from the start of the effective rainfall to the peak. The **time base** is how long the direct runoff lasts.

The flow is split into two parts. **Direct runoff** is the fast response to this storm: water that ran over the surface or through the top of the soil. **Baseflow** is the slow, steady supply from groundwater, which would be there without the storm.

The split cannot be measured, so it is drawn by rule. The simplest rule is a straight horizontal line from the point where the hydrograph starts to rise. Others let the line rise slowly to a point some time after the peak (the N-day methods). For a large flood the choice hardly matters, because baseflow is a small part of the total.
The area under a hydrograph is a volume of water. For the direct runoff, that volume divided by the watershed area is a depth, and this depth is the effective rainfall of Unit 9.

where: direct runoff in each time step: total flow minus baseflow (m³/s)

blocks.p: Dividing by the watershed area $A$ (in m²) gives the depth: $V_d / A$.

A short, intense storm gives a sharp peak; a long, gentle rain gives a broad one. Steep, round or paved watersheds respond fast and high. Flat, elongated or forested ones respond slowly and low. A storm moving downstream along the river piles the water up and raises the peak.

example.q: The flow at the outlet of an 18 km² watershed, read every hour from the start of the rise, is 4, 12, 30, 36, 24, 14, 8 and 4 m³/s. The baseflow is a steady 4 m³/s. Find the volume of direct runoff and the depth of effective rainfall.
steps: Direct runoff, subtracting 4 from each value: 0, 8, 26, 32, 20, 10, 4 and 0 m³/s.
example.a: 360,000 m³ of direct runoff, which is 20 mm (2 cm) of effective rainfall over the watershed. The peak is 36 m³/s, three hours after the rain began, and the time base is 7 hours.

mistakes: **Confusing the hydrograph with the hyetograph.** One is flow against time, the other is rainfall against time.
**Taking lag time and time of concentration as the same.** They are related but defined differently (Unit 13).
**Forgetting to remove the baseflow.** The effective rainfall equals the volume of direct runoff, not of the total flow.
**Treating the peak flow as the size of a flood.** Two floods with the same peak can carry very different volumes, and a reservoir cares about the volume.
notes.ours: The hydrograph is the target of nearly everything we do: hydrologic models and AI models are both judged by how well they reproduce its peak, its timing and its volume. Under a changing climate we also ask how its shape shifts, towards sharper floods and longer low flows.

check.q: After many floods on the same river, which part of the hydrograph looks most alike, and why?
check.a: The recession. It shows how the watershed drains its stored water, which depends on the watershed and not on the storm.

check.q: A 10 km² watershed gives 150,000 m³ of direct runoff. What was the effective rainfall?

notes.title: The unit hydrograph
notes.tldr: The unit hydrograph is the flood that one unit of effective rainfall produces at the outlet. Once we have it, the flood from any storm is found by scaling, shifting and adding.

figure.caption: Building a flood from a unit hydrograph. Each hour of effective rainfall gives its own scaled copy, delayed by one hour; the flood is their sum.

blocks.p: Every watershed turns rain into flow in its own way, but for one watershed that way is fairly stable. The **unit hydrograph** captures it: it is the direct runoff hydrograph caused by one unit depth of effective rainfall, falling evenly over the watershed at a steady rate for a stated duration. Sherman proposed it in 1932.
In Korean textbooks the unit depth is 1 cm. A unit hydrograph always carries its duration: a 1-hour unit hydrograph and a 3-hour unit hydrograph of the same watershed are different curves.

ul: **Constant time base.** Effective rainfalls of the same duration give direct runoff of the same length, whatever their depth.
**Proportionality.** Twice the effective rainfall gives twice the flow at every moment.
**Superposition.** The flows from separate bursts of rain can simply be added.

blocks.p: Together these say that the watershed behaves as a linear system that does not change with time. This is not exactly true, but it is close enough to have been the main tool of flood calculation for ninety years.

Split the effective rainfall into blocks of the unit duration. Each block gives a copy of the unit hydrograph, multiplied by its depth and delayed until the block begins. Adding the copies gives the direct runoff:

where: direct runoff at time step n
effective rainfall in block m, in units of the unit depth
ordinate j of the unit hydrograph

blocks.p: From a measured flood: take a storm of short, even rain, remove the baseflow, find the depth of direct runoff (Unit 11) and divide every ordinate by that depth. Averaging several storms gives a more reliable curve. To change the duration, the S-curve method is used: the unit hydrograph is added to itself again and again to give the response to rain that never stops, and two such curves are subtracted.
For a watershed with no flow record, a **synthetic unit hydrograph** is built from its area, length and slope. The methods of Snyder, the SCS, Clark and Nakayasu are the ones in common use in Korea.

example.q: The flood of Unit 11 came from 2 cm of effective rainfall in one hour and had direct runoff of 0, 8, 26, 32, 20, 10, 4 and 0 m³/s. (a) Find the 1-hour unit hydrograph. (b) Find the direct runoff from a storm with 1 cm of effective rainfall in the first hour and 3 cm in the second.
steps: (a) Divide by 2 cm: $U$ = 0, 4, 13, 16, 10, 5, 2 and 0 m³/s for each cm.
Second hour, $3 \times U$ one hour later: 0, 0, 12, 39, 48, 30, 15, 6, 0.
example.a: The peak is 58 m³/s, four hours after the storm begins. The direct runoff adds up to 200 m³/s, four times that of the unit hydrograph, as it must for 4 cm of effective rainfall.

mistakes: **Applying it to total rainfall.** Remove the losses first (Unit 9), and add the baseflow back at the end.
**Ignoring the duration.** A 1-hour unit hydrograph must be used with rainfall in 1-hour blocks.
**Mixing units of depth.** Korean textbooks use 1 cm; others use 1 mm or 1 inch. Check before multiplying.

**Trusting linearity too far.** In extreme floods water moves faster, and the real peak comes earlier and higher than the unit hydrograph says. On large watersheds the rain is not even, so they are split into sub-basins first.
notes.ours: The unit hydrograph is the simplest rainfall–runoff model: one fixed response curve for a watershed. It is the baseline we keep in mind when we use distributed hydrologic models or train AI models on rainfall and flow, which learn a response that can change with the storm and with the state of the watershed.

check.q: A 1-hour unit hydrograph (for 1 cm) has a peak of 16 m³/s. What is the peak of direct runoff from 2.5 cm of effective rainfall falling in one hour?
check.a: 2.5 × 16 = 40 m³/s, by proportionality.

check.q: A unit hydrograph for 1 cm on an 18 km² watershed must contain what volume of water?

notes.title: Time of concentration and the rational method
notes.tldr: The time of concentration is how long the farthest drop needs to reach the outlet. It tells us which storm duration is the worst for a watershed, and with the rational method it gives a quick estimate of the peak flow.

figure.caption: Left: zones of equal travel time to the outlet. Right: under steady rain the flow rises until the whole watershed contributes, at the time of concentration, and then stays level.

blocks.p: Rain falling close to the outlet arrives within minutes. Rain falling on the far ridge has to cross a hillslope and then travel down the whole channel. The longest of these travel times is the **time of concentration** $t_c$.
It is usually split in two: the **inlet time**, spent flowing over the land to the nearest channel or drain, and the **travel time** along the channel to the outlet.

Imagine rain of a steady intensity. At first only the nearby land feeds the outlet. As time passes, water from farther away joins in and the flow rises. At $t = t_c$ the whole watershed contributes, and from then on the flow stays level.

So a storm shorter than $t_c$ never gets the whole watershed working at once. A storm much longer than $t_c$ does, but by the IDF curve (Unit 6) it has a lower intensity. The worst case lies in between: **a storm that lasts just as long as the time of concentration**.
The time of concentration is rarely measured. It is estimated from the length and slope of the channel with empirical formulas. The one used most for small basins is the Kirpich formula:

where: time of concentration, taken here as the travel time along the channel (min)

blocks.p: Korean textbooks give two more for natural rivers, in the same units:

ul: **Rziha formula**, for upper reaches (slope of 1/200 or steeper): $t_c = 0.833\,L / S^{0.6}$.
**Kraven formula**, for middle and lower reaches (slope of 1/200 or gentler): $t_c = 0.444\,L / S^{0.515}$.

blocks.p: These formulas can differ by a factor of two for the same channel. Choosing one is a judgment, and the result should be read as a rough number.
If the rain lasts at least $t_c$, the peak flow is simply the rate at which rain falls on the watershed, reduced by a factor for the losses:

where: rainfall intensity for a duration equal to the time of concentration (mm/h)

blocks.p: The number 1/3.6 only converts the units. The **runoff coefficient** $C$ is the share of the rain that becomes peak flow: about 0.1 to 0.3 for forest and parks, and 0.7 to 0.95 for roofs and pavement. The method is used for small watersheds, above all for city storm drains.

example.q: A 2.0 km² urban watershed has a main channel 2.5 km long with an average slope of 0.02, and a runoff coefficient of 0.6. The 10-year rainfall is $I = 5{,}400/(t + 30)$ (Unit 6). Estimate the 10-year peak flow, using the Kirpich formula.
steps: Design intensity for that duration: $I = 5{,}400 / (36.3 + 30) = 81.4$ mm/h.
example.a: About 27 m³/s. If the same watershed is paved further, $C$ rises and water also arrives sooner, so $t_c$ falls and the design intensity rises. With $C = 0.8$ and $t_c = 20$ min the peak becomes 48 m³/s.

mistakes: **Dropping the unit factor.** With $I$ in mm/h and $A$ in km², the result needs the factor 1/3.6 to come out in m³/s.
**Using the wrong duration.** The intensity must be read from the IDF curve at a duration equal to $t_c$, not at one hour or one day.
**Using it on a large watershed.** The method assumes even, steady rain over the whole area and ignores storage. It suits small basins of a few km²; larger ones need a hydrograph method.
**Expecting a hydrograph.** The rational method gives the peak only, not the volume or the timing.
notes.ours: Small, fast watersheds are where flood warning is hardest: the time of concentration is the longest lead time that observed rainfall alone can give. This is why our work on urban and flash floods leans on rainfall nowcasting from radar and on AI models that forecast ahead of the rain gauge.

check.q: A storm lasts 10 minutes on a watershed with a time of concentration of 40 minutes. Does the whole watershed contribute to the peak?
check.a: No. Water from the far end is still on its way when the rain stops, so only part of the watershed feeds the outlet at any one time.

check.q: C = 0.5, I = 72 mm/h and A = 1 km². What is the peak flow?

notes.title: Flood routing
notes.tldr: Flood routing follows a flood wave down a river or through a reservoir. Storage on the way makes the peak lower and later, and routing calculates by how much.

figure.caption: A flood entering and leaving a river reach, with the numbers of the worked example. While inflow exceeds outflow the reach stores water; afterwards it gives the water back.

blocks.p: We know the hydrograph at an upstream point. What will it look like some way downstream, or below a dam? Between the two points the water needs room: the river rises, the flood plain fills, the reservoir level climbs. That room is **storage**, and it changes the wave in two ways. The peak becomes lower (**attenuation**) and it arrives later (**lag**).
Routing is the water balance of Unit 3 applied to a river reach or a reservoir, over short time steps. Inflow minus outflow is the rate at which storage changes.

where: inflow at the start and end of the time step
outflow at the start and end
storage at the start and end

blocks.p: The inflows are known, and so are the starting outflow and storage. Two unknowns remain, $O_2$ and $S_2$, so one more relation between storage and flow is needed. Where that relation comes from is the difference between the two cases below.

In a reservoir the water surface is nearly level. Both the storage and the outflow over the spillway depend only on the water level, so storage is a function of outflow alone. One useful result follows: the outflow peaks at the moment it equals the inflow, so the outflow peak always lies on the falling limb of the inflow hydrograph.

In a river the water surface slopes. While the flood rises, more water enters the reach than leaves it, and the surface is steeper than usual. The storage is then seen as two parts: **prism storage** under a line parallel to the bed, which depends on the outflow, and **wedge storage** on top of it, which depends on the difference between inflow and outflow.

where: storage constant, close to the travel time of the wave through the reach
weighting factor between 0 and 0.5; about 0.2 to 0.3 in natural rivers

blocks.p: Putting this into the storage equation gives a rule that is applied step by step:
The three coefficients always add up to 1. $K$ and $x$ are found from a past flood measured at both ends of the reach.

The methods above use only the water balance and are called hydrologic routing. Hydraulic routing also solves the equation of motion of the water (the Saint-Venant equations). It is needed where a downstream level holds the water back: at river junctions, in tidal reaches and on flood plains.

example.q: A river reach has $K = 2$ h and $x = 0.25$. The inflow, read every 2 hours, is 10, 40, 100, 70, 40, 20, 10 and 10 m³/s, and the outflow starts at 10 m³/s. Route the flood with the Muskingum method.
steps: With $\Delta t = 2$ h: $Kx = 0.5$ and $K - Kx + 0.5\Delta t = 2 - 0.5 + 1 = 2.5$.
example.a: The peak falls from 100 to 83 m³/s and arrives 2 hours later. Nothing is lost: the volume under both curves is the same, and the reach only holds the water for a while.

mistakes: **Expecting the outflow peak of a reservoir at the same time as the inflow peak.** It comes later, where the two hydrographs cross.
**Choosing the time step freely.** For the Muskingum method it should lie between $2Kx$ and $2K(1 - x)$, or a coefficient turns negative and the result can swing below zero.
**Thinking that routing removes water.** It reshapes the hydrograph. If the outflow volume differs from the inflow volume, there is a mistake in the arithmetic.
**Using hydrologic routing where water backs up.** Near junctions, tides and gates the flow depends on the level downstream, and a hydraulic model is needed.
notes.ours: Routing is how a forecast at one point becomes a forecast for a whole river, and how the effect of a dam release is judged before the gates open. In large-scale modelling, routing through thousands of river reaches is also what turns gridded runoff, from a land model or from satellite rainfall, into streamflow that can be compared with gauges.

check.q: A reservoir receives a flood with a peak of 500 m³/s. Is the peak outflow over an uncontrolled spillway larger, equal or smaller, and when does it occur?
check.a: Smaller, and later: it occurs when the outflow equals the inflow, on the falling limb of the inflow hydrograph.

check.q: With C₀ = 0.2, C₁ = 0.6 and C₂ = 0.2, find O₂ when I₁ = 50, I₂ = 80 and O₁ = 40 m³/s.

notes.title: Frequency analysis and return period
notes.tldr: How large is the flood we should design for? Frequency analysis answers with a probability: it fits a distribution to the largest value of each year and reads off the value that is exceeded, on average, once in T years.

figure.caption: Thirty annual maxima and a fitted Gumbel distribution, with the numbers of the worked example. Beyond the length of the record the line is an extrapolation.

blocks.p: Nobody can say when the next great flood will come. What a long record can tell us is how often floods of a given size have occurred. Frequency analysis turns that into a rule: a magnitude for each probability. Structures are then designed for a chosen probability, not for the largest flood imaginable.

ul: **Build the series.** Take the largest value of each year: the annual maximum daily rainfall, or the annual peak flow. One value per year keeps the values independent of each other.
**Give each value a probability.** Rank the $n$ values from largest ($m = 1$) to smallest. The Weibull plotting position estimates the probability that rank $m$ is exceeded as $m/(n+1)$.

**Fit a distribution.** Extreme values are not bell-shaped; they have a long tail towards large values. The Gumbel distribution is the classic choice; the GEV and log-Pearson type III distributions are also widely used.
**Check the fit**, with a probability plot and a goodness-of-fit test.
**Read off the design value** for the return period wanted.

blocks.p: As in Unit 6, the return period is the inverse of the exceedance probability in one year, $T = 1/p$. Over the life of a structure the chances add up. The probability that the design value is exceeded at least once in $n$ years is the **risk**:

where: risk: probability of at least one exceedance in n years
return period of the design value (years)

blocks.p: For many distributions the value with return period $T$ can be written as the mean plus a number of standard deviations:

where: mean and standard deviation of the annual maxima
frequency factor, which depends on the distribution and on T

blocks.p: For the Gumbel distribution the frequency factor is:
This gives $K_T$ = 1.30 for 10 years, 2.59 for 50 years and 3.14 for 100 years.

example.q: The annual maximum daily rainfall at a station has a mean of 150 mm and a standard deviation of 50 mm. Assuming a Gumbel distribution, find the 10-year and 100-year rainfall. What is the risk that the 100-year value is exceeded during a 30-year design life?
example.a: 215 mm for 10 years and 307 mm for 100 years. A structure designed for the 100-year rainfall still has a 26% chance, about one in four, of seeing it exceeded within 30 years.

mistakes: **'A 100-year flood comes once every 100 years.'** It has a 1% chance every year. Over 100 years the chance of at least one is 63%, not 100%.
**Extrapolating far beyond the record.** Thirty years of data say little about the 500-year event; small changes in the data move the estimate a great deal. Always ask how long the record is.
**Trusting one distribution.** Different distributions fit the observed range equally well and still disagree in the tail, which is exactly where the design value lies.
**Assuming yesterday's statistics hold tomorrow.** The method takes the climate and the watershed as unchanging. With a warming climate and growing cities, neither is.
notes.ours: This is the centre of our work on climate extremes. We study how design rainfall and floods change when the statistics are no longer stable, how to pool information from many stations, from long reanalysis records and from climate-model ensembles when one record is too short, and how to state the uncertainty honestly.

check.q: A levee is designed for the 50-year flood. What is the chance that it is overtopped at least once in 50 years?
In a 30-year record, what return period does the Weibull plotting position give to the largest value?
check.a: The exceedance probability is m/(n + 1) = 1/31, so T = 31 years.

notes.title: Groundwater and Darcy's law
notes.tldr: Groundwater is the water that fills the pores of soil and rock below the water table. It moves slowly from high head to low head, and Darcy's law says how fast.

figure.caption: A section through the ground, with the numbers of the worked example. Groundwater flows down the slope of the water table and seeps into the river.

blocks.p: Dig a hole and at some depth water collects in it. The level it settles at is the **water table**. Above it, in the **unsaturated zone**, the pores hold both air and water. Below it, in the **saturated zone**, every pore is full. That water is groundwater.
A layer that stores water and lets it move easily enough to supply a well is an **aquifer**: sand, gravel, or fractured rock. There are two kinds.

ul: **Unconfined aquifer.** Its top is the water table, which rises and falls freely with recharge from rain.

**Confined aquifer.** It lies under a layer that hardly lets water through, such as clay, and its water is under pressure. In a well drilled into it the water rises above the top of the aquifer, sometimes above the ground.

blocks.p: Water in the ground does not simply flow downhill, nor from high pressure to low pressure. It flows from high **head** to low head. Head is the level to which water rises in a well: its elevation plus its pressure expressed as a height of water. The drop in head per distance along the flow is the **hydraulic gradient** $i$.
In 1856 Henry Darcy passed water through columns of sand and found that the flow is proportional to the gradient and to the area of the column:

where: cross-section at right angles to the flow (m²)
difference in head between two points (m)
distance between them along the flow (m)

blocks.p: The **hydraulic conductivity** $K$ says how easily water passes through the material. It covers a huge range: 100 m/day or more for gravel, about 1 to 100 m/day for sand, and less than a millimetre a day for clay.
$Q/A = K\,i$ is called the Darcy velocity, but water moves only through the pores, not through the grains. The real average speed is higher:

where: seepage velocity: the real average speed of the water
effective porosity: the share of the volume through which water can move

blocks.p: Where the water table is higher than the river, groundwater seeps into the channel. This is the baseflow of Units 1 and 11, and it keeps rivers flowing through dry weeks. Where pumping pulls the water table below the river, the direction reverses and the river loses water into the ground. The two are one resource.

example.q: Two wells stand 500 m apart along the direction of flow in a sand aquifer with $K = 20$ m/day. Their water levels are 32.0 m and 30.0 m. The aquifer is 15 m thick, and we look at a strip 200 m wide. The effective porosity is 0.25. Find the flow, and the time the water needs to travel between the wells.
example.a: 240 m³/day flows through the strip, and the water takes more than four years to cover 500 m. A river covers the same distance in minutes. This slowness is why groundwater is a reliable reserve in a drought, and why a polluted aquifer takes decades to clean.

mistakes: **Picturing underground rivers and lakes.** Except in caves, groundwater sits in pores and cracks and creeps through them.
**Using the Darcy velocity as the speed of the water.** Divide by the effective porosity; the real speed is several times higher.
**Thinking water flows from high pressure to low pressure.** It flows from high head to low head. Deep groundwater is under high pressure and can still flow upwards.
**Treating K as a precise number.** It changes by orders of magnitude over short distances. A value from one test describes only the ground around that well.
notes.ours: Groundwater is the slow store that carries a region through a drought, and the hardest one to observe. Satellites that measure changes in the Earth's gravity now show how much water a region has gained or lost in total, and we combine such data with models to follow storage through dry years.

check.q: K = 5 m/day, the head falls 1 m over 200 m, and the cross-section is 1,000 m². What is the flow?
It has not rained for a month. Is the river near a high water table gaining or losing water?
check.a: Gaining. Groundwater seeps from the higher water table into the channel, and this baseflow is the river's whole flow in dry weather.
